projects.title: Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain
projects.summary: I built this three module drivetrain as a cheaper way to make a robot that can move in any direction.
projects.cardSummary: I built this three module swerve robot as a cheaper way to move in any direction. It uses common parts, a Raspberry Pi, and Python code that I wrote.

overview.problem: Most competition swerve drives use four modules, special parts, and a lot of money. That can make them hard for smaller teams to build and repair.
overview.method: I used three pods that can each turn, picked parts that were easy to find, and used encoders with Python on a Raspberry Pi to control the steering.
overview.result: The first robot moved smoothly in any direction with three modules, less power, and cheaper hardware. I am using what I learned from it to make version two.

sections.heading: First Robot
sections.body: This was my first time testing the Kiwi swerve idea with three modules. Everything I learned from it is going into the next version.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Kiwi swerve can move in any direction, but it only needs three modules instead of four. I used normal mechanical parts, continuous rotation servos, and encoders to keep the cost down and make repairs easier. I also built the electronics and wrote the Python controls so it could be used for competitions or for teaching robotics.

sections.heading: First Prototype Build
sections.body: The first prototype uses gears and bearings from Amazon and ServoCity, so the pods cost less and the parts are easy to replace. I made the structure with 3D printed parts, CNC cut plates, and normal hardware. Each module has a continuous rotation servo and an encoder for steering feedback. An HTD5 belt connects the servo to the pod, while a longer and lighter HTD2 belt drives the wheel. This lets the drive motor and steering servo stay in place while the pod turns.

sections.heading: Electronics
sections.body: The robot runs on a Raspberry Pi. Each drive motor has a motor driver rated for 10 amps, a servo HAT controls the steering, and a 12 bit encoder board reads the angle of every module. I chose common parts so the system would be easier to fix or change.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: I wrote the controls in Python on the Raspberry Pi. The code takes driver or autonomous commands and calculates what all three modules need to do. It constantly compares the encoder reading with the target angle and corrects the servos while keeping the drive and steering motion lined up.

sections.heading: Second Robot: V2 in Progress
sections.body: I am working on the second Kiwi swerve robot now. It builds on the mechanical design, electronics, and code from the first prototype.

projects.title: AI Eye Animatronic Chatbot
projects.summary: I built a voice activated AI assistant that talks while moving a mechanical eye and eyelids.
projects.cardSummary: I built an AI assistant that talks while moving a mechanical eye and eyelids. I wrote the software and designed the servo mechanism so the movement would not mess with the microphone.

overview.problem: A voice assistant can answer you without feeling like it is really there. Adding moving parts helps, but servo noise can make it harder for the microphone to hear you.
overview.method: I made a small eye mechanism that moves in two directions and connected it to upper and lower eyelids. I also timed the movement with the microphone so the servos would not run while it was listening.
overview.result: The finished prototype can talk, listen, and react with smooth eye movements. The servo noise does not get in the way of a normal conversation.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: I wanted to make a voice activated assistant that could listen and answer while also feeling alive. The main problem was moving the eye without letting the servo noise mess with speech recognition.

sections.heading: Mechanical Design
sections.body: Two hidden servos move the eye up, down, left, and right from a small mechanism mounted to a monitor arm. The upper and lower eyelids are linked so they move together, and I reinforced the pivots to keep everything steady.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: The software handles the wake word, speech recognition, and conversation through a local large language model. Cosine easing makes the eye and eyelids move smoothly, and the servos pause whenever the microphone is listening so they do not add noise.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The finished prototype can wake up, listen, talk, be interrupted, and reset in real time. The smooth eye movement and blinking make it feel more natural without hurting the voice controls.

projects.title: Coaxial Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I designed this small FTC swerve module to use cheaper parts and fit several common hardware systems.
projects.cardSummary: I designed this small swerve module for FTC robots. The second version uses cheaper parts and can mount to GoBILDA, REV, or AndyMark hardware.

overview.problem: A lot of FTC swerve modules are hard to fit inside a robot, expensive to copy, and made for only one type of hardware.
overview.method: I made two small coaxial pod designs. The first one proved that the layout worked, and the second one used more common parts and added more mounting options.
overview.result: The second design stayed small, cost less to repair, and became easier to use with hardware that teams already own.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Many FTC swerve modules are too large or expensive for a team to use. I wanted to make a smaller coaxial pod that could fit inside a competition robot without needing a bunch of special parts.

sections.heading: First Prototype
sections.body: The first design fit inside a cube measuring four inches on each side and combined a printed structure with shafts, gears, and bearings. The drivetrain used four pods with one motor and one servo per module, proving the steering and drive arrangement worked as a complete chassis.

sections.heading: Second Prototype
sections.body: The second version replaced expensive specialty hardware with generic Amazon and AliExpress parts. The module changed from an L shape to a rectangular pod, added mounting support for GoBilda, REV, and AndyMark systems, and grew by less than a quarter inch.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The first pod worked, but it cost about $350 and put the full chassis near $1,300. The second design lowered the cost a lot and made the module easier to mount, repair, and keep developing.

projects.title: Simple Swerve Drive
projects.summary: I made this differential swerve chassis to fit FTC size rules, use common hardware, and stay within an FTC budget.
projects.cardSummary: I built this differential swerve chassis around FTC size and budget limits. I made versions for REV and GoBILDA motors so teams could use parts they already have.

overview.problem: Differential swerve lets a robot move really well, but the gears, size, and number of parts make it hard to use in FTC.
overview.method: I simplified a working differential layout, put the bearings directly inside the gears, and moved the motors around until the chassis fit the size rules.
overview.result: The finished two pod chassis works with either REV or GoBILDA hardware. All four CAD versions are saved in the project repository.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After the 2023 to 2024 NYC FTC championship, I wanted to build a swerve robot between seasons. The hard parts were fitting everything inside the robot and keeping the design affordable enough for FTC.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: I started by studying differential swerve and making a simpler version of FTC 11115's design. I rebuilt the gearbox around M3x45 bolts and bearings placed inside the gears, which cut down on special hardware without changing how the main mechanism worked.

sections.heading: Chassis Iteration
sections.body: The first layout measured 18.25 inches, so the motors were rotated 90 degrees with REV Ultra 90 gearboxes to meet FTC sizing. The chassis used two pods, omni wheels at the other corners, and space for a slide mechanism. Version two added cheaper configurations for REV Ultraplanetary and GoBilda Yellow Jacket motors.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The project is finished. The repository has the full write up, development pictures, and four CAD packages that anyone can download.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: EggWUUUHH
projects.summary: This was Team 9384's CENTERSTAGE robot, which we rebuilt four times to score pixels, launch a plane, and climb.
projects.cardSummary: This was Team 9384's robot for the 2023 to 2024 CENTERSTAGE season. We rebuilt it four times to improve the intake, scoring system, launcher, and climber.

overview.problem: CENTERSTAGE needed one robot to pick up pixels, place them on the backdrop, launch a plane, and climb. We knew the design would have to change as we tested it during the season.
overview.method: We tested each part of the robot on its own and changed the chassis, lift, intake, outtake, and endgame parts whenever a problem showed up in testing or at a match.
overview.result: After four versions, we had a robot that worked reliably and could do every major part of the game.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: For CENTERSTAGE, the robot had to pick up and score pixels on the backdrop, launch a paper plane, and climb at the end of the match. We needed something we could keep changing quickly during the season.

sections.heading: Core Systems
sections.body: The robot used a custom mecanum chassis made from sheet aluminum, a lift built from stacked drawer slides with printed spacers and pulleys, and an active intake with three stages. The backdrop outtake evolved through multiple pivot and pincher designs as testing exposed alignment and reliability issues.

sections.heading: Endgame and Autonomous
sections.body: A plane launcher powered by a spring handled the season's launch task, while an autonomous pixel pincher improved repeatable placement. The final climbing system paired a winch with pivoting hooks and passive rubber assistance.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: After four major versions, we had a reliable competition robot with a strong lift, intake, outtake, launcher, and climber. The CAD and engineering portfolio show how every version changed.

projects.title: Tubba Odometry Pods
projects.summary: I designed these dead wheel odometry pods before small FTC pods were easy to buy, and we used them in competition.
projects.cardSummary: I designed these odometry pods before small FTC pods were easy to buy. We put them on our competition robot and used them to track its position.

overview.problem: We needed the robot to track its position for autonomous and driver assistance, but small FTC odometry pods were not common yet. The choices we had were expensive, hard to fit, or still needed extra parts designed by the team.
overview.method: I designed a compact pod with a passive omni wheel measuring 2 inches in diameter and an encoder with a hollow bore. I built the plates, shaft support, preload system, and mounts around Team 9384's chassis, then helped calibrate the pods as part of the robot's localization system.
overview.result: We installed the finished pods on EggWUUUHH and used them in competition. They tracked the robot consistently, made autonomous paths more accurate, and gave the code position feedback during driver control.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Good odometry takes more than putting an encoder on a wheel. The pod had to fit inside the robot, stay against the field, avoid dragging sideways, protect the sensor, and keep giving the same readings through hits and fast direction changes during a match.

sections.heading: Core System
sections.body: At its center, each pod used a REV encoder with a hollow bore and a passive AndyMark Dualie omni wheel measuring 2 inches in diameter. The tracking wheel rotated independently from the drivetrain, allowing the localization software to measure the robot's actual movement instead of estimating position only from the motion and slip of powered wheels.

sections.heading: Designed From Scratch
sections.body: There was no complete pod we could buy that did what we needed, so I designed the plates, shafts, bearings, wheel support, spring pressure, and chassis mounts as one small assembly. The finished pod fit between the parallel plates on EggWUUUHH, and I saved the full STEP assembly and separate manufacturing files.

sections.heading: Cost and Accessibility
sections.body: Each pod cost about $100 in 2024. The encoder was the most expensive part, while the rest used a printed frame, a standard omni wheel, common bearings, shaft stock, tubing, and regular fasteners. This kept the design practical to repair and reproduce.

sections.heading: Competition Result
sections.body: We installed and calibrated the pods on our competition robot, where they made autonomous movement more repeatable. The live position estimate also gave the control system useful feedback during driver control. Most importantly, the team could trust the readings during a match.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: Crabby
projects.summary: This was Team 9384's POWERPLAY robot, which we rebuilt three times to score cones faster and make the chassis more stable.
projects.cardSummary: This was Team 9384's robot for the 2022 to 2023 POWERPLAY season. We rebuilt it three times to make the lift, claw, turret, and chassis work better.

overview.problem: POWERPLAY was about scoring cones quickly at several heights, so the lift, turret, and chassis all had to work well together.
overview.method: We rebuilt the robot three times. Each version replaced parts that were too slow or flexible with rigid slides, a claw, a stronger frame, and a better turret.
overview.result: The final robot was lower, stronger, and more consistent. Each major change came from a problem we saw during testing or competition.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: POWERPLAY required the robot to collect cones and place them on junction poles at several heights. Fast cycling, accurate alignment, and chassis stability were all critical to competitive performance.

sections.heading: Early Designs
sections.body: The first version paired REV linear slides with an H pattern mecanum chassis and a dual compliant wheel intake. Later iterations increased lift speed, replaced the roller intake with a claw, and introduced a direct drive turret supported by a lazy susan bearing.

sections.heading: Final Revision
sections.body: The final robot used dual rigid slides, an internal bevel gearbox chassis, a larger turret, and a reinforced frame. These changes addressed flex, speed, and alignment problems found during competition testing.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: After three major versions, the robot had a low and stable drivetrain, a faster lift, a reliable claw, and a more accurate turret. Every big change came from something we learned during testing or at a match.

projects.title: OmniBot
projects.summary: We built this low-cost omnidirectional robot as a platform for City Tech students to learn robotics, CAD, programming, and computer vision.
projects.cardSummary: We built this mostly 3D-printed Raspberry Pi robot for under $100. Its three omni wheels, camera, servo, and web controls give club members one platform for learning mechanics, programming, and vision.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: The club wanted an affordable robot that students could build, understand, and change instead of treating it like a closed kit. OmniBot gives members a hands-on way to learn omnidirectional drive code, motors, servos, CAD, 3D printing, Raspberry Pi programming, and local image recognition.

sections.heading: 3D-Printed Build
sections.body: Almost every structural part is printed, including the three-piece chassis, mounts, wheel bodies, and rollers. The rigid wheel bodies use flexible TPU rollers for grip, while heat-set inserts make the robot easier to assemble, take apart, and improve.

sections.heading: Movement and Controls
sections.body: Three omni wheels let the robot move forward, backward, sideways, diagonally, or rotate in place. Students can drive it with a Bluetooth controller or connect to the robot's private Wi-Fi network and use a dashboard from a phone or laptop with keyboard, touch, or gamepad controls.

sections.heading: Camera and Interface
sections.body: A USB webcam supplies live video and images, and a servo lets the camera move. The onboard screen and web dashboard show the camera feed, motor output, servo position, and robot status. Lightweight image recognition is being developed to run locally on the Raspberry Pi rather than through a large language model.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: OmniBot is a working, low-cost club platform with open CAD, code, tests, and a one-command installer. Club members can start by driving it, then study or change the mechanics, controls, interface, camera system, and future vision features.

projects.title: Digital Camera
projects.summary: I built a compact digital camera around an ESP32-S3, then redesigned it with a live viewfinder, physical controls, battery power, and MicroSD storage.
projects.cardSummary: I built this small ESP32-S3 digital camera in two versions. The final version has a live viewfinder, menus, physical buttons, a gallery, battery power, and MicroSD storage.

overview.problem: I wanted to build a small camera from the electronics, enclosure, and software instead of only putting a camera module inside a printed box.
overview.method: I started with a screenless ESP32-S3 camera, learned from that version, and rebuilt it around a Freenove ESP32-S3 Media Kit with a display, controls, battery, storage, and a custom case.
overview.result: The final camera works as a self-contained handheld device with a live preview, menus, a photo gallery, and full-resolution images saved to a MicroSD card.

sections.heading: From V1 to V2
sections.body: V1 used a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense without a screen. I could take photos, but I had to use a Wi-Fi page to download them and could not see the picture before pressing the shutter. For V2, I changed to the Freenove ESP32-S3 Media Kit and added the features that the first version was missing.

sections.heading: Viewfinder and Controls
sections.body: V2 has a 1.14-inch color screen, a live viewfinder, menus, a directional control, and physical buttons. I used LVGL and TFT_eSPI for the interface, and the software scales the camera feed down for the preview while keeping the full image for the saved photo.

sections.heading: Storage and Gallery
sections.body: The camera saves full photos to a DCIM folder on a MicroSD card. I also made an onboard gallery so I can review saved pictures directly on the camera instead of moving the card or connecting to another device.

sections.heading: Case and Power
sections.body: I designed and printed a compact case around the screen, camera board, controls, and a 1500 mAh LiPo battery. The repository includes the complete enclosure as a STEP file and an editable Fusion 360 archive so the design can be rebuilt or changed.

sections.heading: Open Documentation
sections.body: I documented the parts, wiring warning, Arduino board settings, exact display libraries, setup process, firmware, and CAD files in the repository. The current battery percentage is not reliable, so I also documented that limitation instead of presenting it as an accurate charge reading.

projects.title: TrainUI XL
projects.summary: I built this full-size departure board to show live New York City train arrivals, alerts, weather, time, and Raspberry Pi information in one place.
projects.cardSummary: I built this 10.1-inch departure board for live New York City train arrivals, service alerts, weather, and system information. It runs on a Raspberry Pi Zero W and starts by itself when powered on.

overview.problem: I wanted one always-on screen where I could quickly check New York City train information without opening an app or using another tablet.
overview.method: I made a fullscreen interface for the original Raspberry Pi Zero W, connected it to official MTA realtime feeds, and wrote an installer where the user picks a train and station.
overview.result: TrainUI starts by itself and shows arrivals, service alerts, weather, the time, and information about the Raspberry Pi.

sections.heading: Live Information
sections.body: The screen shows arrivals in both directions, service status and alerts for the selected route, New York City weather, the current time, connection information, and the health of the Raspberry Pi. The public MTA and weather feeds do not need API keys.

sections.heading: Raspberry Pi Kiosk
sections.body: The reference build uses an original Raspberry Pi Zero W and a 10.1 inch HDMI monitor in a custom three part printed enclosure. The software runs fullscreen and is designed to stay readable from a distance.

sections.heading: Installation and Reliability
sections.body: The installer runs with one command and lets the owner choose a supported train and station. It also sets up automatic startup, stops the screen from going blank, and checks the internet connection so it can keep running for a long time.

projects.title: ZeroG Hydra 3D Printer
projects.summary: I am building this large CoreXY printer for good print quality, automatic calibration, and reliable hardware.
projects.cardSummary: I am building this large CoreXY printer for reliable prints and automatic setup. It has a three point moving bed, several toolhead sensors, and Klipper controls.

overview.problem: Large printers can be harder to keep consistent and repair, especially when the bed still has to be adjusted by hand.
overview.method: I used a rigid CoreXY frame, a bed that levels itself at three points, electronics that are easy to reach, and several toolhead sensors to make extrusion more consistent.
overview.result: The Hydra is still being built, but the main motion system, automatic calibration, and monitoring hardware are already working.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After building and changing several printers, I wanted to make a larger one that focused on print quality, strong parts, and useful sensors instead of only trying to be fast.

sections.heading: Motion and Bed
sections.body: The Hydra uses CoreXY motion and a floating bed that moves at three separate points. The printer adjusts those points during automatic tramming, so the bed stays rigid while the firmware fixes its alignment before a print.

sections.heading: Electronics and Toolhead
sections.body: An electronics bay under the printer houses the USB hub, controller, power supply, solid state relay for the bed powered by 110 volts, and the Linux computer running Klipper. A Filimetrix design inspired the toolhead, which adds dual filament sensors, a cutter, Beacon eddy current probing, lighting, a touchscreen, a Phaetus Rapido hotend, and a Clockwork 2 extruder.

sections.heading: Status
sections.body: I am still working on the printer. It is already the biggest printer project I have taken on because of the large build area, automatic calibration, toolhead sensors, and extrusion system.

projects.title: Delta 3D Printer
projects.summary: I rebuilt this delta printer with motors that have encoder feedback, direct drive extrusion, and a strong CPAP cooling system.
projects.cardSummary: I rebuilt this delta printer to make it faster and more consistent. I added direct drive extrusion, motors with encoder feedback, nozzle probing, and strong remote cooling.

overview.problem: The delta frame could move fast, but friction, weak cooling, and hard calibration kept the prints from coming out clean every time.
overview.method: I made several toolhead versions before switching to direct drive, motors with encoder feedback, stronger cooling from a remote blower, and a probe that uses the nozzle.
overview.result: The rebuilt printer still has the speed of a delta machine, but now the extrusion, cooling, and calibration are more consistent.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: I wanted the speed of a delta printer without giving up print quality. I used stepper motors with encoder feedback, a light effector, and strong part cooling while working through the calibration and space problems that come with a delta machine.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: I kept the TEVO Little Monster frame, power supply, and solid state relay. The first Bowden setup added friction and left marks on the prints, so I later switched to direct drive and mounted a CPAP blower on the frame with a light hose going to the effector.

sections.heading: Toolhead Iterations
sections.body: Version two combined the ducts, hotend, extruder, and probe but exposed problems with airflow and the probe offset. Version three lowered the hotend and center of gravity, improved the ducts, and added a detachable nozzle probe. NEMA 17 motors with encoder feedback and a TFT35 KlipperScreen completed the control system.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The finished machine prints quickly and consistently. It has encoder feedback on the motors, direct drive extrusion, better calibration, powerful cooling, and a custom screen interface.

projects.title: Voron V0.2990
projects.summary: I modified this small Voron to print faster, cool parts better, and be easier to watch and repair.
projects.cardSummary: I modified this small Voron to print faster and be easier to maintain. I changed the toolhead, cooling, sensors, filtration, lighting, and electronics layout.

overview.problem: The small Voron worked well, but heat, extrusion flow, monitoring, and hard to reach electronics held it back during long or fast prints.
overview.method: I changed the toolhead for higher flow, added outside cooling, enclosure sensors, air filtration, print failure monitoring, and wiring that is easier to reach.
overview.result: The changes made the printer faster, easier to repair, and safer to watch during long prints.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: I started with the community designed Voron and looked for the parts that were holding it back. Most of my changes went into extrusion, cooling, monitoring, filtration, and making the electronics easier to reach.

sections.heading: Performance Upgrades
sections.body: A custom toolhead combines a stronger extruder and high flow hotend for printing around 225 to 350 mm/s with travel speeds up to 650 mm/s. An external 12032 fan increases part cooling without adding excessive moving mass.

sections.heading: Reliability and Usability
sections.body: The enclosure adds active carbon filtration, a chamber thermistor, reinforced panels with RGB lighting, upgraded hinges, and a camera for failure detection and timelapses. A filament runout and extrusion sensor monitors material flow, while a larger Mini12864 display improves local control.

sections.heading: Serviceability
sections.body: The electronics are mounted on DIN rails behind a hinged rear door, and a quiet Noctua fan keeps them cool. These changes make the printer faster, safer, and much easier to work on.

projects.title: Self Balancing Robot
projects.summary: We built three self balancing robots from parts at school using Raspberry Pi and Arduino boards.
projects.cardSummary: We built three self balancing robots with Raspberry Pi and Arduino boards. They use a gyro and PID code to stay upright while moving.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The club wanted a controls project we could build with parts that were already at school. A self balancing robot made it easy to see how the gyro, motor control, and tuning all work together.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: We made three robots. One uses a Raspberry Pi with Python, and the other two use Arduino Nano and Uno boards. Each robot has a motor driver, DC motors, a gyroscope, and a custom chassis.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: A PID controller reads the robot's angle, keeps both motors working together, and corrects the robot when it starts to fall. We kept tuning the code and changing the wheel position, chassis shape, and center of gravity until each robot became more stable.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: All three robots can balance while standing still or moving forward and backward. Club members can use them to learn PID control, programming, and how the mechanical design changes the balance.

projects.title: Crab Crawler
projects.summary: We built three small ESP32 walking robots to teach wireless programming, sensors, and servo movement.
projects.cardSummary: We built three small walking robots with ESP32 boards, cameras, screens, and two servos each. Students can change the code and learn how the walking motion works.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: We wanted a robot that students could use to learn ESP32 programming, cameras, sensors, and servo boards without making the build too complicated.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: We made three crawlers with 3D printed frames and two servos on each robot. Each one also has an ESP32 CAM for wireless control and video, an OLED screen, and a separate servo driver.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: The code controls the walking motion, screen information, camera connection, and wireless commands. We changed the walking pattern and body shape together until the two servo mechanism had better grip and stayed stable.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The crawlers can walk, stream live video, and show their status on the screen. They use only a few parts and simple code, so students can understand them and add their own ideas.

projects.title: TrainUI Mini
projects.summary: After building TrainUI XL, I turned the same idea into a small, low-cost ESP32 e-paper project that I could use to teach City Tech club members.
projects.cardSummary: I adapted my larger TrainUI project into a small ESP32-S3 e-paper display for the City Tech club. It gives students a useful way to learn microcontrollers, display programming, and public data feeds without requiring a large budget.

sections.heading: Why I Made a Mini Version
sections.body: After building the larger TrainUI XL for myself, I wanted to reuse the idea in something much smaller for the City Tech AI & Automation Club. The club does not have a large budget, so an ESP32-S3 board with a built-in 2.13-inch e-paper display made the project cheaper, simpler, and easier to teach than another Raspberry Pi and full-size monitor.

sections.heading: A Teaching Tool With a Purpose
sections.body: TrainUI Mini was more of a teaching exercise than a completely new product. Connecting it to a project I had already built gave every lesson a real purpose: by the end, the board could show useful train arrivals, service status, temperature, time, and connection information instead of only running isolated example code.

sections.heading: ESP32 and E-Paper Lessons
sections.body: I used the project to explain how ESP32 development boards are configured and programmed through Arduino IDE, how they connect to Wi-Fi, and how embedded code controls hardware. I also taught how e-paper behaves differently from a regular screen, including the way the display is refreshed and how information has to be arranged clearly in a very small space.

sections.heading: Using Live Public Data
sections.body: The software connects directly to public MTA and Open-Meteo data. This let me explain how a small device requests information from an online service, reads the response, selects the useful fields, and turns that data into a screen layout. The display does not need a phone app, account, separate server, or API key.

sections.heading: Setup and Result
sections.body: On first startup, the ESP32 creates its own setup network so the user can enter Wi-Fi details and choose a train and station. Those choices stay saved on the board. The finished project is a compact, useful display and a repeatable lesson for learning ESP32 boards, e-paper, Wi-Fi setup, APIs, and embedded interface design.

projects.title: AutoCAD I
projects.summary: This class taught me the basics of AutoCAD through drawings, dimensions, layouts, and printing.
projects.cardSummary: This class taught me the basics of making clear technical drawings in AutoCAD. I worked on dimensions, layouts, title blocks, and printing.
projects.classRundown: Completed 2D drafting exercises, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final while practicing dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotting.

overview.problem: I needed to learn how to turn the shape of a part into a drawing that was accurate, easy to read, and ready to print.
overview.method: I completed drawing exercises, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final while practicing dimensions, title blocks, layouts, and plotting.
overview.result: By the end of the class, I was faster in AutoCAD and my drawings were cleaner and easier to understand.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: I completed classwork, homework, quizzes, a midterm, and a final while learning the basics of technical drafting.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The work included 2D geometry, object snaps, repeated features, dimensions, sheet layouts, title blocks, and saving drawings as PDFs.

sections.body: This certificate recognizes my completion of the 2026 NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech summer internship.

sections.heading: Mecanum Test Chassis
sections.body: I started with a simple mecanum chassis during the first week. It gave us a working platform for testing the new Systemcore and Motioncore electronics, A301 motors, battery, sensors, controls, and drivetrain layout.

sections.heading: A301 Swerve Development
sections.body: I spent the next several weeks designing, printing, machining, assembling, and testing custom two-motor swerve modules. Three main revisions simplified the steering, improved the gear layout, and led to the final CNC-machined pods.

sections.heading: Final Swechanum Robot
sections.body: The final robot combines the original lower mecanum structure with four powered swerve pods above it. The swerve system uses eight A301 motors and does all of the driving, while the lower mecanum wheels remain as passive support wheels. The linked repository documents the CAD, build history, and development path for all three stages.

projects.title: A301 Chassis Swechanum
projects.programSummary: This was a six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. I did the mechanical work on the robot while another intern worked on the code, and I also learned how to use the machines in the shop.
projects.summary: This was the final robot from my six week NYC FIRST internship. It combines the mecanum base with four custom A301 swerve modules.
projects.cardSummary: I built this four module swerve robot during my six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. It combines the mecanum base with four custom A301 swerve modules.

overview.problem: We needed a working robot to test the early Systemcore and Motioncore hardware, and it also had to be easy for students to understand and change. We wanted to see if four A301 swerve modules could steer and drive together as a complete FTC chassis.
overview.method: I worked on the mechanical design, CAD, CAM, 3D printing, manufacturing, and assembly. Another intern wrote the code, and I used ideas and feedback from my supervisor and the rest of the team when I changed the design.
overview.result: The final robot drove with four powered A301 swerve pods and eight motors. As far as I know, it was the first tested and working open source FTC chassis to use four A301 swerve pods with Systemcore and Motioncore.

sections.heading: Six Weeks From a Test Base to a Full Robot
sections.body: I built the first plywood mecanum prototype in one day. I spent the rest of the first two weeks testing it, changing the layout, and making sure the electronics and drivetrain worked. I was also doing the required training for the CNC machines, laser cutter, and 3D printers during that time. I spent the final four weeks mainly designing, building, and testing the swerve system. During the last assembly week, I cut the finished mecanum parts from metal so the full robot could go together.

sections.heading: Open Source Project
sections.body: The CAD and robot code are open source. Students, teams, or anyone else can download the files, look through the design, and build their own version at home. As far as I know, this is the first open source A301 swerve project with a full chassis that has been built and tested.

sections.heading: What Made It Different
sections.body: People had made individual A301 swerve modules before, but as far as I know, nobody had finished a full chassis that used four of them to steer and drive one robot. This robot uses four V3 pods. Each pod has one A301 motor for driving and another for steering, and the motors are controlled through Systemcore and Motioncore.

sections.heading: From Belt Steering to Direct Steering
sections.body: The first module used belts to turn the pod. My supervisor suggested making it more like an FRC swerve module, so I redesigned it with the steering motor directly in the center of rotation. The motor shaft now turns the pod without a steering belt, giving it a simple one to one connection.

sections.heading: Designed for Education
sections.body: We also wanted the robot to be useful for teaching. A new student can start with mecanum movement, basic motor control, IMUs, and other sensors before trying swerve code and steering calibration. The modules are open enough that students can see the gears, wheel drive, and steering move while the robot is running.

sections.heading: Working as a Team
sections.body: I did the CAD, CAM, printed prototypes, manufacturing, and mechanical assembly. Another intern wrote the software, while my supervisor and coworkers gave me ideas and feedback during the build. I used their input and what I saw during testing to make each new mechanical version.

sections.heading: Why the Robot Looks Slow
sections.body: I designed the drivetrain for 2,000 RPM gearbox cartridges, but because this was alpha testing, we only had the 500 RPM versions. That made the test robot about four times slower than it was meant to be. It still showed that all four pods could steer together and drive the full chassis.

sections.heading: Final Configuration
sections.body: The top drivetrain has four powered swerve pods and eight A301 motors in total. The four mecanum wheels underneath are not powered and only stayed on the robot as support wheels. There are no caster wheels, and the swerve assembly does all of the driving.

projects.title: A301 Swerve Module
projects.programSummary: This was a six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. I did the mechanical work on the robot while another intern worked on the code, and I also learned how to use the machines in the shop.
projects.summary: I spent the final four weeks of my internship making this two motor swerve pod through three main versions.
projects.cardSummary: I designed this A301 swerve module during the last four weeks of my internship. Three main versions led to the final direct steering design used on the robot.

overview.problem: The Systemcore robot needed a small pod that could both drive and steer with A301 motors. It had to work reliably without being too complicated for a student who was just learning swerve.
overview.method: I spent the final four weeks making three main versions of the module. Testing led me from belt steering to a direct motor connection, and I kept changing the gears and shape to make the pod smaller, easy to see, and simple to put together.
overview.result: I machined four V3 pods and installed them on the final robot. V3.1 keeps the working 3.1:1 drive reduction and direct steering, but fixes the bearing hole that was too tight during assembly.

sections.heading: Four Weeks and Three Major Iterations
sections.body: After I finished the mecanum chassis, I spent the last four weeks on the swerve modules. I designed, printed, assembled, and tested three main versions. Each one made the steering simpler, changed the gear layout, and made the pod smaller without hiding how it worked.

sections.heading: Drive and Steering Layout
sections.body: Each pod uses two A301 motors. One motor drives the wheel through two 1:1 spur stages and a 3.1:1 offset bevel set. The second motor sits directly at the center of rotation and turns the complete lower module.

sections.heading: From Belts to Direct Turning
sections.body: The first prototype used a belt to turn the pod. After getting the idea to make it more like an FRC swerve module, I moved the A301 steering motor to the center so its shaft could turn the module directly. This got rid of the steering belt and worked well enough to use on the final chassis.

sections.heading: From Printing to CNC
sections.body: I used printed parts to check the shape and fit before machining the plates. When I CNC machined V3, the main bearing hole came out too tight and squeezed the bearing enough to stop it from turning smoothly. I fixed the fit in V3.1 without changing the drivetrain layout that already worked.

sections.heading: Designed for Students
sections.body: I wanted to handle the harder design problems so a student could focus on learning from the finished module. The mechanism stays simple, and the openings around the gears let students see the drive and steering parts move. They can use it while learning motor control, steering calibration, encoders, IMUs, and swerve programming.

sections.heading: Wheel and Future Ratchet
sections.body: The wheel and TPU tread can print together on a multimaterial printer, so the tread does not need a separate assembly step and still grips the FTC mat well. I also added mounting holes for a ratchet that did not arrive in time. It can be installed later without redesigning the pod.

sections.heading: Open Source Project
sections.body: The module CAD and test code are open source. Anyone can download the files, look through every version, and use them to start their own build. This module is part of the first open source A301 swerve project that was fully built and tested.

sections.heading: Mechanical and Software Roles
sections.body: I did the module CAD, CAM, printed prototypes, manufacturing, and mechanical assembly. Another intern wrote the code, while my supervisor and coworkers gave ideas and feedback that helped me change the design.

projects.title: STEM Research Academy Robot Lab
projects.programSummary: I was a mentor for two high school students during this six week STEM Research Academy program. They came in with limited robotics experience, so the mentors helped them learn the mechanical, electrical, and programming skills they needed to finish the robot.
projects.summary: I mentored two high school students as they learned the skills needed to build, wire, and program a full robot. The finished mecanum robot carries the two smaller robots they made during the first half of the program.
projects.cardSummary: I mentored two high school students while they learned how to design, build, wire, and program robots. We spent three weeks learning with smaller robot kits, then three weeks building the final robot that carries both minibots.

overview.problem: The two students needed to learn more than how to assemble a robot. They needed enough experience with design, manufacturing, electronics, Linux, and programming to understand the full build and make it work themselves.
overview.method: The first three weeks were spent teaching and building smaller robot kits. During the last three weeks, the students and mentors used those skills to build the full 3TSahur mecanum robot and turn the first two kits into minibots that ride on the larger robot.
overview.result: The final robot drives on four mecanum wheels, carries both minibots on one ramp, streams video from a Logitech C270 camera, and can be controlled from a phone or computer through its own Raspberry Pi WiFi network.

sections.heading: My Role as a Mentor
sections.body: I mentored two high school students during the six week program. I taught CAD, CAM, and 3D printing with two other mentors. I personally taught both students the electronics, wiring, firmware, microcontrollers, Linux, and Raspberry Pi setup they needed for the robots.

sections.heading: The First Three Weeks
sections.body: We spent the first three weeks teaching the main skills and building robot kits. The students learned how to model parts, prepare them for manufacturing, print them, assemble the robots, wire the electronics, and start working with the code. Those kits later became the two minibots carried by the final robot.

sections.heading: Electronics and Wiring Lessons
sections.body: I showed both students how to use 12 volts for the motors and how to use buck converters to step 12 volts down to 5 volts for the Raspberry Pi and servos. We covered common grounds, motor drivers, safe power wiring, soldering, connectors, and how to check everything before turning it on.

sections.heading: Signals, Firmware, and Data
sections.body: I also taught them how PWM controls motors and servos, how USB moves data between devices, and how the robot sends commands and camera information. They learned how to flash firmware to microcontrollers, connect the boards, and understand what the different signals and data connections were doing.

sections.heading: Linux and Raspberry Pi Setup
sections.body: Both students learned how to install and set up Raspberry Pi OS, use Linux, connect the hardware, and run the robot software. I walked them through enough of the setup that they could understand how the robot starts, connects to its own network, and runs the controls.

sections.heading: The Last Three Weeks
sections.body: We spent the final three weeks building the large robot. It uses a Raspberry Pi 4, four independently driven mecanum wheels, one ramp moved by servos, a Logitech C270 camera, and a browser based control screen. The Raspberry Pi makes its own WiFi network, so the robot can be driven from a phone, tablet, or computer without internet.

sections.heading: What the Students Programmed
sections.body: The students wrote the mecanum drive code and the servo code for the ramp. The WiFi setup and browser control screen were harder for them because they did not have much experience yet, so the mentors helped heavily with those parts. We walked them through how the network, Raspberry Pi, robot controls, and user interface worked together instead of expecting them to already know it.

sections.heading: The Two Minibots
sections.body: The two robot kits from the first half of the program became minibots that the large robot carries around. The big robot has one servo controlled ramp for moving them on and off, and the minibots use ESP32 S3 and ESP32 CAM microcontrollers on their own local networks.

sections.heading: What the Students Finished With
sections.body: By the end of the six weeks, the students had worked through the full process of designing, making, wiring, setting up, and programming a robot. They did not only put together a premade commercial kit. They learned how the mechanical parts, power, signals, firmware, Linux setup, and software all connect in a complete robot.

projects.title: A301 Mecanum Chassis
projects.programSummary: This was a six week internship at the NYC FIRST STEM Center at Cornell Tech. I did the mechanical work on the robot while another intern worked on the code, and I also learned how to use the machines in the shop.
projects.summary: I built the first plywood mecanum chassis in one day, then spent the next two weeks testing it and making it better.
projects.cardSummary: I built the first plywood version of this mecanum chassis in one day during my internship. I spent the next two weeks testing it, improving it, and preparing the final metal version.

overview.problem: Before starting the custom swerve work, we needed a simple robot for testing the early Systemcore and Motioncore electronics, A301 motors, battery, controls, sensors, and the amount of space everything needed.
overview.method: I built the first plywood mecanum prototype in one day. I used the rest of the first two weeks to test it, change the layout, finish my shop training, and make the robot reliable and easy for students to understand.
overview.result: The finished chassis worked as both a drivetrain and a robot students could learn from. During the final assembly week, I cut the finished design from metal so it could hold the nose drawer and connect to the rest of the robot.

sections.heading: A One Day First Prototype
sections.body: I designed and built the first plywood mecanum chassis in one day. Getting a simple robot moving that quickly let us test the new motors, controllers, battery, sensors, and software before starting the harder swerve work.

sections.heading: Two Weeks of Refinement and Training
sections.body: Even though the first prototype only took a day, I used the first two weeks to fix the layout, try different materials, and make sure everything worked. I was also doing the required training for the CNC machines, laser cutter, and 3D printers that I used later in the build.

sections.heading: Why the Motor and Wheel Pivot Out
sections.body: I designed each motor and wheel assembly so it can pivot outward from the chassis. This lets a team change the A301 gearbox cartridge without taking the whole robot apart, and it makes the new motor and its mounting setup easy to see. Opening the side also gives direct access to the motor wiring and wheel locking collar, which makes testing, debugging, and adjustments much easier.

sections.heading: Omnidirectional Drive
sections.body: The four mecanum wheels let the chassis drive forward and backward, move sideways or diagonally, and turn in place by changing what each wheel does. This made it useful for testing the control hardware and early drivetrain code.

sections.heading: From Test Platform to Final Structure
sections.body: The mecanum robot showed us how the A301 motors, 18 volt battery pack, Systemcore, Motioncore, wiring, and chassis size worked together in a real build. During the final week, I made the finished chassis from metal so the nose drawer and the rest of the robot could be assembled.

sections.heading: Designed for Education
sections.body: Mecanum gives new students an easier place to start. They can learn basic motor control, sideways movement, IMUs, and other sensors before moving on to the harder swerve modules and code. The hardware is left easy to see so students can understand how everything goes together and what each part does.

sections.heading: Open Source Project
sections.body: The mecanum CAD and robot code are open source. Anyone can download the files, see how the robot was built, and use them to start a drivetrain of their own.

sections.heading: Mechanical and Software Roles
sections.body: I did the CAD, CAM, prototypes, manufacturing, and mechanical assembly. Another intern wrote the code, while my supervisor and coworkers gave us ideas and feedback during the build.
